become.verb type: **linking (copular)** in the main sense — it joins the subject to a noun or adjective rather than acting on anything (*she became a citizen*, *the neighborhood became quieter*), and it is dynamic, so the progressive is fine: *he is becoming impatient*. The formal *suit / befit* senses (*that green becomes you*, *such language hardly becomes a judge*) are **stative** and reject the progressive: ✗ *that green is becoming you*.
become.transitivity: **Linking** in senses 1–2 — what follows is a subject complement, not an object, and *become of* is a fixed intransitive pattern used almost only with *what/whatever* (*whatever became of the family next door?*). Senses 3–4 are **transitive** with a person as object, and that object is obligatory: ✗ *the short haircut became*.
become.passive: **no.** A subject complement can never move to subject position: ✗ *a citizen was become by her*. The transitive *suit/befit* senses are stative and refuse it too: ✗ *you are become by that deep green*, ✗ *a judge is hardly become by such language*.

come.verb type: action — dynamic verb of motion and arrival (*my parents come over on Sundays*, *spring has come late*). Also **linking** in a short fixed list only — *come true, come loose, come undone, come clean, come free* — which is not productive: ✗ *she came tired*.
come.transitivity: **intransitive** in every documented sense. Anything that looks like an object arrives through a preposition: *come from Ohio*, *come to forty-two dollars*, *come across her old letters*, *come up with a name*, *come down with the flu*. ✗ *she came the station* is impossible.
come.passive: **no** — an intransitive verb has no passive: ✗ *the package was come two days early*. The prepositional idioms resist the prepositional passive as well: ✗ *her old letters were come across*, ✗ *the flu was come down with*.

outrun.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the literal speed one (*a deer can outrun a coyote*) and the figurative outpacing one (*costs have outrun the budget*). No linking or stative use.
outrun.transitivity: **transitive** only, and the object is obligatory: *she outran every other sprinter*, *demand tends to outrun supply*. ✗ *the deer outran* is incomplete — compare plain *run*, which is happy with no object.
outrun.passive: **yes**, though the active is far more common: *the coyote was easily outrun*, *supply has been outrun by demand for three quarters*.

overcome.verb type: action — dynamic: getting past a difficulty (*she overcame a serious injury*) or defeating an opponent (*the visitors overcame a twelve-point deficit*). After *be*, the participle in *overcome with grief* shades into an adjective describing a state.
overcome.transitivity: **transitive** in every sense, with an obligatory object — a problem, a feeling, or an opponent: ✗ *recruits overcome* on its own. The object is the difficulty itself, not the person who has it: *overcome their fear of heights*, not ✗ *overcome the recruit of his fear*.
overcome.passive: **yes**, and very common — *a twelve-point deficit was overcome in the fourth quarter*. Sense 2 is passive-only in practice: *two firefighters were overcome by smoke*, *he was overcome with relief*. The form after *be* is always the participle: ✗ *he was overcame*.

overrun.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: spreading over something (*weeds overrun that lot every summer*), going past a limit (*the meeting overran its slot*), or rolling past a stopping point (*the jet overran the runway*).
overrun.transitivity: **both** — transitive with an object in most uses (*ants have overrun the pantry*, *the project has overrun its schedule*), but intransitive when the limit is left unsaid: *long agendas always overrun*.
overrun.passive: **yes**, and the infest sense is most often met in the passive: *by August the garden had been completely overrun*, *the place is overrun with tourists*. No passive of the intransitive use: ✗ *the slot was overrun by the meeting* in the sense of *the meeting overran*.

rerun.verb type: action — dynamic: broadcasting something a second time (*the station reruns the pilot every holiday weekend*) or carrying a process out again (*we reran the numbers*).
rerun.transitivity: **transitive** only, with an obligatory object — an episode, a test, a program, a vote: ✗ *the lab has rerun* is incomplete.
rerun.passive: **yes**, and it is the ordinary way to say it in official and lab contexts: *the court ordered the election to be rerun in three counties*, *that episode has been rerun a dozen times*.

run.verb type: action — dynamic; also **linking** in the fixed *run low / run late / run high / run deep / run dry* (*supplies run low*, *the well has run dry*), which reports a level rather than any movement.
run.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the movement, flow, route, and extent senses (*she runs two miles*, *the faucet ran all night*, *the bus runs every fifteen minutes*), transitive in the management and operation senses (*run a bakery*, *run the sample*, *run the numbers*).
run.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the store is run by her sister*, *the sample was run twice*. No passive of the intransitive ones: ✗ *two miles were run by her* in the ordinary sense, ✗ *low was run by supplies*.
